https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/01/russ.text: Russia expelled a group of Hungarian diplomats on Thursday after Hungary ordered 10 Russian diplomats out last month, marking a sharp break from the era of former Premier Viktor Orbán, who maintained closer ties with Moscow than any other EU leader.Hungary's chargé d'affaires Gábor Gergics was summoned to Russia's foreign ministry and informed that staff from the Hungarian embassy in Moscow and consulates in St Petersburg and Kazan had been ordered to leave within two weeks.Moscow described Hungary's original 8 September expulsion as a "baseless and openly unfriendly" act.Budapest acknowledged Moscow's decision but said it stood by its position."Hungary is not interested in an escalation of diplomatic tensions. But we stand by our decision, taken on national security grounds. Our missions continue to operate in full, and Hungary will maintain its diplomatic presence in Russia," the Hungarian foreign ministry wrote on X.Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said at the time of the initial expulsion that the Russian diplomats "had been engaged in activities in Hungary that are unacceptable for diplomats under the Vienna Convention."The mutual expulsions follow a shift in Hungarian foreign policy since Prime Minister Péter Magyar took office earlier this year.At the end of August, the new government's guidance to its delegation at the UN General Assembly officially described Russia as a threat to Hungary and to the "global order," condemned its ongoing all-out war in Ukraine and affirmed support for Ukrainian sovereignty and its right to self-defence.Hungary is also seeking to improve relations with Kyiv, although Budapest is blocking the opening of new EU accession negotiation clusters with Ukraine to secure concessions on the rights of the country's Hungarian minority.Orbán, who was in power for 16 years until his party Fidesz' loss in general elections this April, openly sympathised with the Kremlin and refused to join other EU member states in expelling Russian diplomats after Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022.He made multiple visits to Moscow after the invasion and repeatedly used Hungary's veto in the European Council to block Ukraine-related initiatives.Magyar has promised "pragmatic" relations with Moscow during his tenure.

https://www.forbes.ro/sabin-dima-founder.text: Artificial intelligence is making it possible, for the first time, to run companies with no employees at all. But who takes responsibility for them? This tension shaped the dialogue between Sabin Dima, Founder & CEO of humans.ai, and Andrada Morar, VP Customer Experience, Global Partnerships & Tech Alliances at UiPath, at Forbes România Business Bridges 2026, the event organized by Forbes Romania at Forbes on Fifth in New York. Dima recently invested in a startup with a programmatic name, Zero Humans. "What fascinates me about this new world is the fact that, for the first time, you are able to create a company with no humans at all," the humans.ai founder said. "I'm looking at this technology with which, for the first time, you can really achieve the impossible from an economic perspective. If this cost almost goes to zero, it means that for the first time we are going to have new business models that were impossible before," Sabin Dima explained. Andrada Morar drew the line where regulation begins. "When you think about regulated industries, I think zero humans would be a non-starter. There should still be a human to take accountability," the UiPath executive said. "You're not just working in an experiment or in a sandbox anymore. You use these technologies for business outcomes. Nobody goes to a board and says, I've automated 200 processes," Morar explained. The healthy starting point, in her view, is not what can be automated, but what business problem needs to be solved. And problems keep moving. "In any company, small or big, a process is not something that you define once and it stays like that, because people leave, companies grow, software gets replaced," Andrada Morar said. UiPath is working on agents that look across a company's processes as a whole and identify where they can be completely reimagined, or even eliminated. Dima sees a more radical option: instead of retrofitting old companies, AI makes it possible to build new ones from scratch. He gave the example of a telecom operator, whose real asset is its license, leveraged today with thousands of employees, and which could be rebuilt with an entirely different structure. The discussion then turned to Romanian entrepreneurs and the American market. Morar, who returns to Romania often, praised the technical expertise in Bucharest, but also in Cluj and other cities. She also identified a reflex that holds them back. "One thing I've seen in Romanian companies is a lot of humbleness. That feeling of 'I'm just starting, I'm in Romania, I'm not in Silicon Valley'," she observed. The example she gave was UiPath's own founder. "Daniel never started a company for the Romanian market. He jumped on a plane and went to India, then to Japan, which is still one of the hardest markets. For us, it became one of the strongest, because we were there and we solved the problem the market had. If you start with the right mindset, building a company that's global and not limiting yourself to the European market just because it's comfortable, you're already a step ahead," Andrada Morar said. Dima went further, arguing that the road to America is simpler than it seems. "The United States has tons of problems and the budget for them. The American market gives you both the problems and the solutions. It's ridiculous, but it's so easy for a Romanian entrepreneur to create a startup that serves the US market," he said. For UiPath, the next challenge comes from a crowded market. More and more vendors promise the same thing, and clients need to see the differences under the hood. "Nobody thinks about the tech vendor in isolation. They think about the problem they need to solve and what they need to show the board when it comes to their AI investment. That's how decisions are being made," Morar explained.

https://www.dw.com/en/as-russia-steps-up.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5Nv2l Data centers are essential for maintaining online services Image: Serjunco/Westend61/IMAGO Advertisement Hackers and power outages were once the largest threat to Ukraine's data centers. Now, it is the buildings themselves that are in the cross hairs. Since early September, Russia has been targeting these centers, which house the physical infrastructure needed to store digital information, systematically. Digital infrastructure in and around the capital Kyiv was already affected but after the attacks, several television channels and streaming services were temporarily unavailable. Subscribers to several cable networks also reported that they had difficulties connecting. Why is Russia targeting Ukrainian data centers? The servers and computer systems needed to store data and keep online services operating smoothly are a crucial target because if they are damaged, it can have a nationwide effect. All online systems, ranging from news portals, state registries, banking and finance, need functioning data centers to operate smoothly. Ukrainian Minister of Foreign Affairs Andrii Sybiha said Russia had targeted major Ukrainian data centers to disrupt the flow of information. "As Russia isn’t achieving its goals on the battlefield, it is seeking new ways to destabilize life in Ukraine and terrorize civilians." Has Russia changed its approach in its war with Ukraine? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Could Ukraine go offline? Despite widespread damage caused by Russian attacks , experts do not believe the country risks having a complete internet blackout. Telecommunications expert Oleksandr Glushchenko told DW that this was because the entire sector was quite decentralized. "The industry was never regulated in Ukraine, and no multi-million licenses were required,” he explained. "Entering the market was very affordable, which is why thousands of businesses started offering their services." He added that Ukrainians could choose between multiple providers — and in some cases up to 10. This competition, he said, meant that Ukraine had "some of the best internet provider services in the world." At the same time, he noted, damage caused by kinetic attacks could cause certain providers to "go dark" while repairs took place. Meanwhile, Ukrainian lawmaker Oleksandr Fediienko, who is a member of the parliamentary Committee on National Security, Defense and Intelligence, posted similar sentiments on the social network Facebook: "Will the internet disappear in Ukraine? Of course not. The infrastructure will be restructured, and alternative sites will be established." He added that the Russian attacks made no sense because Ukrainian providers were able to restore service so quickly. Lessons from Latvia: How to deal with Russian hybrid threats To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Serhii Beskrestnov, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy's advisor on defense technology, said that Russia's attacks on Ukrainian data centers were part of a wider campaign. "They've already been scaring us with claims that there won't be food or fuel, and now they're scaring us with the prospect of losing internet access," he wrote on Facebook. How can data and devices be protected? Glushchenko said that even if a server was destroyed, its data would be available from other data centers where it was stored, including abroad. "The system can automatically switch to a different data center," he explained. He pointed out that telecommunications companies also stored copies with cloud services offered by providers such as Google and Amazon. What happens when data centers lose power? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Oleksandr Olshanskyi, the founder of the Ukrainian web hosting provider MiroHost and also the head of the leading Ukrainian IT service company Internet Invest, told the Ukrainian news agency RBC-Ukraine that his data center had been almost totally destroyed but that this had not made a major difference. He said that the vast majority of his clients remained unaffected, as they could fall back on operation capacities in Poland and the Czech Republic. "I'm only left with about 150 out of 20,000 to 25,000 clients, who for some reason did not shift, duplicate or secure their data," he explained. Tech experts have recommended that Ukrainian data centers place a higher priority on decentralization, saying they should be as spread out as possible geographically, and also that data should be cloned and secured in other data centers abroad. Moving infrastructure into underground spaces could also be a solution, but this would translate into extra costs for customers. "We've grown accustomed to having the fastest and cheapest internet in Europe, and the best technical support," Fediienko said but pointed out that this was "about to change." Beskrestnov also expected the price of internet services to rise soon, to cover the costs of repairing damage to infrastructure. This article was originally published in Ukrainian.
